title: They told you all paths lead to God.
paragraphs:
They told you all paths lead to God.
It sounded kind. Inclusive. Peaceful.

But what if that idea…
is the most dangerous lie you’ve ever believed?

Because not every path heals.
Some paths just make brokenness feel beautiful.

Some paths teach you to silence your mind—
but never cleanse your soul.

Some paths train your body—
but ignore your sin.

Some paths whisper softly,
“You are already enough.”
But the Bible doesn’t whisper that.

It reveals something deeper.
Something uncomfortable.
“For all have sinned and fall short of the glory of God.” (Romans 3:23)

Not some.
Not the worst.
All.
Here’s the tension most people avoid:

If sin is real—
then not every path can fix it.

If sin separates us from God—
then not every road leads back to Him.

You can’t meditate sin away.
You can’t discipline it out.
You can’t outgrow it.
Sin isn’t just a mistake.
It’s a condition.
Go back to the beginning.

In Genesis 11, humanity tried to build a tower to heaven—
the Tower of Babel.

Brick by brick.
Effort by effort.
Pride stacked on pride.

It looked spiritual.
It looked unified.
It looked powerful.
But God came down and stopped it.
Why?

Because they were trying to reach God
without surrendering to Him.

That’s the danger of false paths—
they look like progress…
but they’re rooted in rebellion.
And here’s where it gets personal.

You can be sincere—
and still be wrong.

You can feel spiritual—
and still be lost.

You can follow a path that feels peaceful—
and still end in separation from God.

“There is a way that seems right to a man,
but its end is the way to death.” (Proverbs 14:12)
Let that sit.

Now here comes the turning point.
The interruption of grace.
Because Christianity is not about humans climbing up to God.
It’s about God coming down to us.

Not a ladder.
A rescue.

Not self-improvement.
A Savior.
Jesus didn’t enter history to offer one option among many.
He made a claim that cuts through every philosophy, every religion, every human effort:

“I am the way, the truth, and the life.
No one comes to the Father except through Me.” (John 14:6)
Not one of many.
The way.

That statement is either offensive…
or it’s the most loving truth ever spoken.

Because if Jesus is the only way—
then God didn’t leave you guessing.
He didn’t hide the path.
He became the path.
Look at the cross.

That wasn’t symbolic.
That was substitution.

Your sin—placed on Him.
Your guilt—carried by Him.
Your punishment—absorbed by Him.
“God shows His love for us in that while we were still sinners, Christ died for us.” (Romans 5:8)

Not when you fixed yourself.
Not when you became worthy.
While you were still broken.
And this is where every other path falls short.
Because no other path deals with sin at the root.
No other path offers forgiveness that is paid in full.

No other path gives you righteousness as a gift—
not something you earn, but something you receive.
“For by grace you have been saved through faith… not a result of works.” (Ephesians 2:8-9)

So no—
not every spiritual path leads to God.
But here’s the hope that changes everything:
God made a way for every person.

Not through performance.
Not through perfection.
Not through rituals or self-mastery.
Through Jesus Christ alone.

Right now—yes, you—
you are standing at a crossroads.
Not between many equal roads.
But between two:

👉 Trusting yourself
or
👉 Surrendering to Christ

One path says,
“Climb.”

The other says,
“It is finished.”
And deep down, you already know this:

You don’t need another method.
You don’t need another system.
You need mercy.
You need forgiveness.

You need a Savior who doesn’t just guide you—
but carries you.
So here’s the invitation:

Turn from sin.
Turn from self.
Turn toward Jesus.

Not halfway.
Not casually.
Fully.

Because the narrow road isn’t narrow to restrict you—
it’s narrow because it leads to life.

Sit with it.
Pray honestly.
Ask God to reveal truth.
And if you’re ready—
Say it:

“Jesus, I surrender.
I can’t save myself.
I trust You.”
Because eternity is not a theory.
It’s a destination.

And today…
you choose the road.
We tell the stories that shame tried to erase.
